web_title: 6. 6-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Behind the 40% Margin — Lease Leverage, Dilution & Cash Forensics
question: What do six years of P&L, balance-sheet, cash-flow, and shareholding forensics reveal about Afcom's financial durability and promoter alignment?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion; operating cash flow after lease payments and receivables is the only truth an airline balance sheet cannot hide.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: From FY21 to H1 FY27, Afcom Holdings posted one of the fastest sales ramps in Indian air cargo [1, 17]. Revenue grew from ₹13.89 crore in FY21 to ₹241.01 crore in FY25 and ₹583.00 crore in FY26 [1, 17]. H1 FY27 sales reached ₹417.00 crore [1, 20]. Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) rose from 21% in FY25 to 28% in FY26 [1, 16]. Yet the balance sheet and cash-flow statement show three key weak spots [1, 9, 10]. Those risks are **Ind AS 116 lease debt**, **weak CFO-to-PAT conversion**, and **repeated share dilution** [1, 9, 10].

web_blocks.caption: Afcom Holdings: 6-Year Financial Forensics & Cash Conversion (FY21–FY26 + H1 FY27, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue grew 42x from FY21 to FY26 and H1 FY27 CFO improved to ₹49.47 Cr (55% of PAT; *FY25 equity restated from ₹195.51 Cr to ₹180.00 Cr on Ind AS transition; H1 debtor days annualized), yet cumulative FY25–H1 FY27 investing outflows reached -₹678.38 Cr, keeping FCF deeply negative.

web_blocks.html: First, under Ind AS 116, Afcom's 96-month dry leases add ~₹306.35 crore of Right-of-Use (ROU) assets, which declined to ₹280.49 crore by September 2026 [28, 30]. They also add **~₹338 crore of FY26 lease debt** inside total FY26 borrowings of ₹400.70 crore [10, 30]. By September 2026, consolidated borrowings stood at ₹398 crore, covering ₹76.39 crore of standalone ex-lease debt plus ₹269.41 crore of non-current lease liabilities and current lease obligations [20, 28]. Transitioning from Indian GAAP to Ind AS also restated FY25 PBT down by ₹13.67 crore (from ₹65.21 crore to ₹51.54 crore) and FY25 equity down by ₹15.51 crore (from ₹195.51 crore to ₹180.00 crore) [30]. Second, FY26 CFO lagged PAT badly at 29.5% (₹36.00 crore vs. ₹122.00 crore PAT). In H1 FY27, however, **CFO improved to ₹49.47 crore (55.0% of ₹89.95 crore standalone PAT)** as trade receivables stabilized at **₹134.52 crore** vs. ₹135.76 crore in March 2026 [28]. Yet headline September 2026 cash of ₹92.31 crore hides a tight liquidity squeeze. Exactly **₹87.16 crore sits restricted in QIP monitoring accounts**, leaving just **₹5.15 crore in unrestricted current accounts and cash on hand** [28]. Meanwhile, trade payables fell from ₹28.23 crore to ₹3.24 crore, and H1 investing outflows hit -₹214.46 crore across ₹89.07 crore of lease deposits, ₹82.42 crore of capital advances, and ₹45.27 crore of subsidiary investments and loans [28].

web_blocks.caption: Afcom Holdings: Shareholding Shift & Institutionalization (Sep 2024 – Sep 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Promoter stake fell 733 bps (42.73% to 35.40%) from May 2026 QIP/preferential dilution plus promoter-group open-market disposals, while DII ownership jumped from 0.85% to 7.61%; further warrant conversions run through June 2027.

web_blocks.html: Third, the shareholding table shows steady equity dilution alongside notable promoter-group equity turnover [1, 29, 30]. Promoter stake held at 42.73% through June 2025, then slipped to 40.61% in March 2026 and 35.40% by September 2026 [1]. While the bulk of this 7.33-point drop came from **new share sales**—the May 2026 QIP (26.31 lakh shares, ₹199.84 crore), a preferential issue (12.10 lakh shares, ₹104.47 crore), and warrant conversions (including 1.25 lakh warrants converted on November 12, 2026 at ₹863.17/share, with remaining warrants exercisable through June 17, 2027)—BSE insider filings confirm it was **not purely dilution** [10, 12, 27, 28]. Promoter-group member Thiagaraja Annamalai executed open-market disposals (51,120 shares for ₹8.41 crore in September 2026, plus a further disposal disclosed on November 25, 2026), while co-founder Wg. Cdr. Jaganmohan Manthena attempted an off-market 10.43 lakh share (3.61%) transfer to promoter Manjula Annamalai at ₹800/share (deferred October 29 due to lock-in) before resigning from the Board and Audit Committee on November 12, 2026 [27, 29, 33]. Capt. Deepak Parasuraman kept his core stake, and DII ownership rose to 7.61% led by Bandhan Mutual Fund, Abakkus, and Ashish Kacholia [1, 12, 19]. Fresh equity eased near-term debt risk, yet future per-share gains require CFO to fund fleet growth internally.

Lease accounting under Ind AS 116 also shapes cash flows [13, 14]. ROU assets stood at ₹306.35 crore in FY26 (₹280.49 crore in September 2026) against ~₹338.00 crore of FY26 lease debt [13, 14, 28]. Lease principal payments go under Financing Cash Flow, not Operating Cash Flow [14]. Meanwhile, lease interest (₹32.00 crore in FY26; ₹10.94 crore in H1 FY27) and depreciation (₹53.00 crore in FY26; ₹33.06 crore in H1 FY27) hit the P&L [10, 14, 28]. Even with H1 FY27 CFO improving to ₹49.47 crore, heavy lease deposits (₹89.07 crore), capital advances (₹82.42 crore), and subsidiary investments/loans (₹45.27 crore) pushed H1 Free Cash Flow to -₹164.99 crore [28].

The gap between 28% ROCE in FY26 (up from 21% in FY25) and persistent negative Free Cash Flow (-₹170.71 crore in FY26; -₹164.99 crore in H1 FY27) defines Afcom's balance-sheet puzzle [1, 14, 15, 28]. Accounting returns look strong when planes fly full, and H1 FY27's 55% CFO-to-PAT conversion proves working capital is no longer deteriorating as fast as revenue [1, 28]. Still, with only ₹5.15 crore in unrestricted operating bank balances outside QIP monitoring accounts and ₹326.39 crore tied up in other non-current assets/deposits, free cash flow—not ROCE—limits self-funded growth [28]. Full-year FY27 must show sustained >50% CFO/PAT conversion alongside positive unrestricted liquidity without another equity raise [10, 12, 28].

book_paragraphs: Now let's put on our forensic-accounting hat and look behind Afcom's headline numbers. Between FY21 and FY26, revenue multiplied more than fortyfold, from ₹13.89 crore to ₹583 crore, and return on capital employed reached 28%. Yet when you and I open the audited balance sheet and cash-flow statement, four forensic realities emerge—starting with the Ind AS transition that restated FY25 pre-tax profit down by ₹13.67 crore and equity down by ₹15.51 crore to ₹180 crore.

Second, Afcom's aircraft sit on the balance sheet under Ind AS 116 as ₹306.35 crore of FY26 Right-of-Use assets (₹280.49 crore by September 2026) paired with roughly ₹338 crore of lease liabilities inside ₹400.70 crore of total FY26 borrowings. Third, while FY26 operating cash flow was just ₹36 crore against ₹122 crore of net profit as trade receivables ballooned to ₹135.76 crore, H1 FY27 marked an encouraging inflection: receivables stabilized at ₹134.52 crore and H1 CFO climbed to ₹49.47 crore (55% of PAT). Fourth, however, ₹214.46 crore of H1 investing outflows left free cash flow at -₹164.99 crore, and ₹87.16 crore of September 2026's ₹92.31 crore cash sat restricted in QIP monitoring accounts—leaving just ₹5.15 crore in unrestricted operating cash.

book_callouts.title: DILUTION & GOVERNANCE WATCH: PROMOTER STAKE AT 35.40%
book_callouts.text: Promoter ownership dropped from 42.73% at IPO to 35.40% by September 2026—driven mainly by QIP/preferential dilution, but compounded by promoter-group open-market disposals (Thiagaraja Annamalai), warrant conversions running through June 2027, and co-founder Jaganmohan Manthena's November 12, 2026 board exit.

book_subsections.title: Decoding the Promoter Stake Decline, Insider Sales & DII Entry
paragraphs: At first glance, seeing promoter ownership drop from 42.73% in September 2024 to 35.40% in September 2026 raises an immediate red flag. Did the founders cash out? The filings show a mixed picture. The largest portion of the drop occurred in the June 2026 quarter, coinciding directly with the May 2026 QIP of ₹199.84 crore, a ₹104.47 crore preferential share allotment, and warrant conversions—while domestic institutional investors led by Bandhan Mutual Fund, Abakkus, and Ashish Kacholia lifted DII ownership from under 1% to 7.61%. However, BSE insider disclosures also show open-market sales by promoter-group member Thiagaraja Annamalai (including ₹8.41 crore in September 2026 and a further disposal on November 25, 2026), alongside co-founder Wg. Cdr. Jaganmohan Manthena's deferred 3.61% off-market transfer to Manjula Annamalai and his November 12, 2026 resignation from the Board and Audit Committee.

Even with Captain Deepak Parasuraman retaining his core stake, serial equity dilution and ongoing warrant conversions through June 2027 remain a double-edged sword. Equity raises lifted net worth to ₹758.40 crore and funded ₹678 crore of cumulative investing outflows from FY25 through H1 FY27. Going forward, the single biggest forensic test for Afcom is whether H1 FY27's improved 55% CFO-to-PAT conversion holds so that the fourth and fifth narrowbodies—and any future widebodies—are funded internally rather than via another share issuance.

book_subsections.title: The Price-Blind Business Quality Verdict
paragraphs: Before we ever look at a stock chart or a valuation multiple, we owe ourselves an honest verdict on business quality. Afcom is not a fragile shell company—it has built real operational credibility, a profitable India–ASEAN niche, and institutional backing. At the same time, 30% cash conversion, 85-day receivables, heavy lease liabilities, and reliance on cyclical charter demand mean this is not an effortless asset-light compounder. It earns a conditional cyclical pass: strong execution, with cash conversion and fleet discipline firmly on watch.

book_subsections.title: How Ind AS 116 Lease Accounting Masks Cash Burn
paragraphs: Let us linger on one accounting detail that trips up almost every generalist investor looking at an airline: Ind AS 116 lease accounting. On Afcom's FY26 balance sheet, Right-of-Use assets sit at ₹306 crore against ₹338 crore of lease liabilities. Under accounting rules, lease depreciation of ₹53 crore and lease interest of ₹32 crore flow through the income statement, while the actual principal portion of monthly aircraft lease payments is tucked away inside Financing Cash Flows.

That means Reported Operating Cash Flow actually flatters a dry-leased airline compared to a company that pays rent straight through operating expenses. Yet even with that accounting tailwind, Afcom's FY26 operating cash flow was just ₹36 crore against ₹122 crore of reported net profit—a 29.5 percent conversion ratio—while investing cash outflows hit -₹206.71 crore. Until receivables shrink from 85 days and security deposits stop absorbing every rupee of profit, Afcom's financial engine remains dependent on external capital.

book_subsections.title: Reconciling 28 Percent ROCE With Negative Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: On paper, a 28 percent Return on Capital Employed in FY26—up from 21 percent in FY25—looks like the hallmark of a capital-efficient compounder. Yet in that same fiscal year, Afcom generated -₹170.71 crore of free cash flow once ₹206.71 crore of investing outflows were netted against ₹36 crore of operating cash flow.

How can both numbers be true at once? Because ROCE measures operating profit against deployed capital on the balance sheet, whereas free cash flow captures the upfront cash consumed by aircraft lease deposits, entry-into-service capex, and 85-day customer receivables while the fleet is tripling in size. That gap is precisely why our price-blind verdict is CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL rather than an unconditional pass.

With Chapters 1 through 6 complete, our price-blind foundation is locked. Afcom is a genuine operational breakout on the income statement—scaling revenue fortyfold from FY21 to FY26—yet its 29.5 percent CFO-to-PAT conversion, 85-day receivables, ₹338 crore lease liabilities, and serial equity dilution place it squarely in the CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL tier.

Keep that six-year financial table in mind whenever you hear an analyst cite Afcom's 40 percent EBITDA margin. Margin without cash conversion is only half the story, and Q3 FY27 will show whether working-capital friction is finally easing.
